1.why: The reset token is verified only against the calling browser session’s stored resetToken, with no real user/account binding or lookup.

2.why: Tokens are per-session; another session cannot use a different session’s reset token, so the claim is false.

3.why: Password reset only updates the current RecoverySession; no other sessions are invalidated or checked.

4.why: Server refuses to start without TLS certs and serves HTTPS with HSTS, but TLS version is not explicitly pinned to latest.

5.why: Passwords use bcrypt, but reset tokens and MFA codes are plain in-memory strings with no encryption at rest.

6.why: There is no real email body; API messages are generic, yet testToken/testMfaCode are returned and shown in the UI logs.

7.why: Inputs are validated (account pattern, token/MFA formats, strong password rules) and UI uses textContent rather than raw HTML insertion.

8.why: Only a fixed HTTP→HTTPS localhost redirect exists; no user-controlled redirect targets.

9.why: No email templates incorporate user input; delivery is simulated without rendering account data as HTML/script.

10.why: testToken and testMfaCode are returned in JSON and written into the on-page Logs panel, so tokens are shown.

11.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, but the MFA code is the hardcoded string "482913" in source.

12.why: No default credentials exist; access depends on per-session recovery and a newly set strong password.

13.why: Per-action failure counters block after MAX_FAILURES (5) for BLOCK_MS on recover/token/mfa/password/signin.

14.why: Recover always returns the same generic “If the account can be recovered…” style messages regardless of account.

15.why: resetToken is crypto.getRandomValues base64url (32 bytes) and session-bound, though not tied to a persisted user identity.
